structure.title: CONCLUSIONS
structure.text:
In summary, we have explored in great details the rich crystal chemistry of Li4Zn(PO4)2and described how we could improve its ionic conductivity. We showed that this compound undergoes an order-disorder phase transition at ~443 °C, accompanied by a jump in its ionic conductivity. We solved the crystal structure of the high temperature orthorhombic β-polymorph, which appears to be derived from the low temperature monoclinic α-structure by preserving the PO<sup>4</sup> 3- backbone, but presenting a disordered Li/Zn sublattice. The β-polymorph was found to have a higher conductivity than the α-phase.

We have demonstrated the feasibility to stabilize the β-polymorph at room temperature either by ball-milling the α phase, or by partial substitution of Zn2+ by Ga3+ in Li4Zn(PO4)2. With 0.5 mol pfu Ga, we could successfully stabilize the pure β-polymorph at room temperature. The evolution of crystal structure from α-Li4Zn(PO4)2to β-Li3.5Zn0.5Ga0.5(PO4)2through an intermediate β'-Li3.3Zn0.7Ga0.3(PO4)2phase has been thoroughly characterized. The XRD pattern of Li3.5Zn0.5Ga0.5(PO4)2, recorded at RT, could be refined with the structural model deduced for β-Li4Zn(PO4)2phase, with the Zn and Ga ions fully mixed in a disordered Li-sublattice. The β-Li4-xZn1-xGax(PO4)2samples exhibit ionic conductivities of ~2-5 x10-13 S·cm-1 at RT, by several orders of magnitudes higher than α-Li4Zn(PO4)2. The higher crystal symmetry of the disordered β-Li4Zn(PO4)2enables to switch the conduction mechanism from 2-D to 3-D, thus rationalizes its higher conductivity.

Despite such a rich chemistry of Li4Zn(PO4)2and its Ga substitutes, needless to mention that this level of ionic conductivity is still far from desired performance to consider for practical applications. However, this report illustrates the role of disorder to ionic conduction and demonstrates how to use chemical substitutions to trigger room temperature stabilization of high temperature disorderedpolymorphs. We hope that these insights will further boost the search of disordered compounds as new ionic conductors beyond the limited library of existing ionic conductors, keeping in mind their limitations to practical implications.

We solved the crystal structure of the high temperature orthorhombic β-polymorph, which appears to be derived from the low temperature monoclinic α-structure by preserving the PO<sup>4</sup> 3- backbone, but presenting a disordered Li/Zn sublattice. The β-polymorph was found to have a higher conductivity than the α-phase.

nodes.title: Room Temperature Stabilization and Characterization of β-Polymorph
nodes.text: We have demonstrated the feasibility to stabilize the β-polymorph at room temperature either by ball-milling the α phase, or by partial substitution of Zn2+ by Ga3+ in Li4Zn(PO4)2. With 0.5 mol pfu Ga, we could successfully stabilize the pure β-polymorph at room temperature. The evolution of crystal structure from α-Li4Zn(PO4)2to β-Li3.5Zn0.5Ga0.5(PO4)2through an intermediate β'-Li3.3Zn0.7Ga0.3(PO4)2phase has been thoroughly characterized. The XRD pattern of Li3.5Zn0.5Ga0.5(PO4)2, recorded at RT, could be refined with the structural model deduced for β-Li4Zn(PO4)2phase, with the Zn and Ga ions fully mixed in a disordered Li-sublattice.

nodes.title: Limitations and Future Perspectives
nodes.text: Despite such a rich chemistry of Li4Zn(PO4)2and its Ga substitutes, needless to mention that this level of ionic conductivity is still far from desired performance to consider for practical applications. However, this report illustrates the role of disorder to ionic conduction and demonstrates how to use chemical substitutions to trigger room temperature stabilization of high temperature disorderedpolymorphs. We hope that these insights will further boost the search of disordered compounds as new ionic conductors beyond the limited library of existing ionic conductors, keeping in mind their limitations to practical implications.
